draft.title: Weighing strategies with criteria
card: A strategy is a plan to deal with a problem, such as flooding or a shortage of clean water. Each option has strengths and weaknesses, so judge them all against three criteria.
Environmental
does it work? The effect on land, water, air and living things.
Economic
what does it cost? The price of the option and the money it saves or earns.
Social

who benefits, and can it last over time? The effect on people's health, safety, jobs and way of life, now and for future generations. Then recommend one option and explain its likely effects, including the downsides it still has.
draft.remember: Judge options on environmental, economic and social criteria, including whether they work, what they cost, who benefits and whether they last.

a.q: Why does a geographer judge each management option against several criteria before recommending one?
opts: Doing well on one criterion can hide harm on another
Using all three criteria can remove a strategy's downsides
Each criterion ranks the options in the same order
Cost decides the choice, and the other criteria are extras
a.why: An option can look good on cost but harm the environment or people, and checking every criterion shows this. Comparing does not remove downsides: the chosen option still has some, which is why the card says to explain its likely effects.
a.clue: Think about an option that is cheap but causes harm.

b.q: A council on the Great Ocean Road is deciding how to protect a coastal town from erosion. A sea wall would be expensive and may speed up erosion on nearby beaches. Which statement uses an economic criterion?
opts: The sea wall costs a lot to build and maintain
The sea wall may speed up erosion on nearby beaches
The sea wall would keep homes safe for residents
The sea wall would change the habitat of shore birds
b.why: Cost to build and maintain is a money matter, so it is an economic criterion. Erosion on beaches and shore bird habitat are environmental effects. Safety for residents is social, which is the tempting option because homes also have a dollar value.
b.clue: Homes are worth money, but what is that statement really about?

a.best: Doing well on one criterion can hide harm on another

b.best: The sea wall costs a lot to build and maintain

problems.detail: The card ties 'does it work?' only to the environmental criterion and 'can it last?' only to the social criterion. Effectiveness is not purely environmental: a flood or water strategy works by protecting people. Whether a strategy can last also spans all three parts. Students may learn a misleading mapping.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear answer each. The card wrongly pairs 'does it work?' only with environmental criteria and 'can it last?' only with social criteria, which could mislead students.

proposal.title: Judging environmental management
card: A management strategy is a plan to deal with an environmental problem, such as flooding or a shortage of clean water. Whether it works and whether it can last are judged across all three criteria below.
Environmental
the effects on land, water, air and living things.
Economic
what it costs to build and run, and the money it saves or earns.
Social
who benefits or loses, and the effects on people's health, safety, jobs and way of life.
proposal.remember: Weigh each option on environmental, economic and social criteria, asking if it works and if it can last.

a.q: A council asks whether its new flood levee can last. Which question fits this best?
opts: Will it still protect people and be affordable in 30 years
Will it stop next winter's flood from reaching homes
Which residents gain the most from it being built
How much money will it cost to build this year
a.why: Lasting means the strategy keeps working over time, and that covers people, money and the environment together. Stopping next winter's flood is about whether it works now, not whether it can keep working for years.
a.clue: Which question looks far into the future?

b.why: Cost to build and maintain is a money matter, so it is an economic criterion. Erosion on beaches and shore bird habitat are environmental effects. Safety for residents is social, which is the tempting option because homes also have a dollar value.
b.clue: Homes are worth money, but what is that statement really about?

version.title: Judging environmental management
card: A management strategy is a plan to deal with an environmental problem, such as flooding or a polluted river. Each option is judged on three kinds of criteria, and one that does well on one kind can do poorly on another.
Environmental
how it affects land, water, air and living things. Does it work for the environment, and will that last?
Economic
what it costs to build and maintain, and the money it saves or earns. Does it pay off, and can it be paid for over time?
Social
how it affects people's health, safety, jobs and way of life, and who benefits. Does it work for people, and will it keep their support?
version.remember: Ask whether each option works and can last for the environment, for the budget and for people.
